morphology.motility: Non-motile — distinguishes it from most other Bacillus species

habitat.naturalHabitat: Soil, where spores persist for decades
habitat.hostAssociation: Primarily infects herbivores (cattle, sheep, goats); humans infected incidentally
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Endospores are extremely resistant and persist long-term in soil

microscopy.stain: Gram stain; polychrome methylene blue (McFadyean stain) for capsule
microscopy.appearance: Large Gram-positive rods with square ends, central spores

culture.growthCharacteristics: Facultative anaerobe; non-hemolytic, unlike most other Bacillus species
culture.colonyMorphology: Large, gray-white, non-hemolytic colonies with irregular "Medusa head" edges

identificationClues: Large Gram-positive rods in bamboo-stick chains
Central endospores that do not swell the cell
Capsule visible with McFadyean (polychrome methylene blue) stain

virulenceFactors: Anthrax toxin — protective antigen, edema factor, lethal factor
clinicalImportance.transmission: Contact with infected animals/animal products; inhalation of spores; ingestion of contaminated meat; historically used as a bioterrorism agent
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Endemic in regions with unvaccinated livestock; occupational risk for those handling animal hides/wool; inhalational anthrax has high mortality if untreated
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Non-motility and non-hemolysis distinguish it from the closely related but far less dangerous Bacillus cereus

examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Non-motile and non-hemolytic, unlike the otherwise similar Bacillus cereus
